name: Ink, Tea and Woodblocks: A Thousand Years of Japan
description: From a court lady's long story in Kyoto to Hokusai's wave and Kurosawa's samurai: Japan's arts, rituals and screens across more than a thousand years.

checkpoints.name: Court and capital
checkpoints.note: Sumo and the kimono belong to Japan's early centuries, and woodblock printing is used for Buddhist texts. In 794 the capital moves to Kyoto, opening the Heian period. Gion Matsuri begins in 869, and around 1010 the court lady Murasaki Shikibu writes The Tale of Genji.

checkpoints.name: Warriors and quiet arts
checkpoints.note: The samurai, whose rise began in the Heian centuries, come to dominate Japanese politics. Alongside them grow quieter arts: Noh, a masked drama refined in the 1300s, and the Japanese tea ceremony, which takes shape in the 1500s as a discipline of calm and hospitality.

checkpoints.name: The Edo peace
checkpoints.note: Under the Tokugawa shogunate a long peace brings Himeji Castle, the lively theatre of Kabuki, the poet Matsuo Basho and the colourful ukiyo-e prints of city life. Hokusai's Great Wave off Kanagawa appears around 1831, and the Treaty of Kanagawa of 1854 opens Japan to foreign ships.

checkpoints.name: A modern empire
checkpoints.note: After 1868 the Empire of Japan modernises quickly. Its new cinema soon produces the director Akira Kurosawa, born in 1910, and the actor Toshiro Mifune, born in 1920, who will carry Japanese film abroad, while Haruki Murakami is born in 1949.

checkpoints.name: Screens and novels
checkpoints.note: Rashomon (1950), Tokyo Story (1953) and Seven Samurai (1954) bring Japanese cinema to audiences abroad. Haruki Murakami becomes one of the most translated novelists, and the Tokyo Skytree, opened in 2012, shows a country still building on a grand scale.
